name: Sunless tan injections ('tan jabs')

lead: Tan jabs are unlicensed melanotan injections that people use to darken skin with little or no sun. The appeal is a deeper, longer-lasting tan without hours in the sun or a bed.

Melanotan peptides are synthetic analogues of alpha-MSH, the hormone that drives melanin production, so melanocytes make more pigment. They have never been approved as tanning drugs. Health agencies began warning against them in 2007 and the US FDA issued a warning letter in 2009; related approved drugs exist for other uses.

paras: They are sold online and in some gyms and salons rather than through licensed channels. Users typically report combining them with some sun or UV exposure to bring colour in, with a gradual darkening over weeks.

Reported effects include flushing and nausea, and mole darkening or other mole changes; a 2009 BMJ report linked an unlicensed tan jab to mole changes. The melanoma evidence is unclear. They are unlicensed for tanning, products are unregulated, and agencies advise against use.

angle.text: Melanotan, a synthetic alpha-MSH analogue, is injected to prompt melanocytes to make more melanin and darken skin with less or no sun. Its pigment-raising action is established; the tanning use is unlicensed and health agencies have warned against it since 2007.

lead: "Tan jabs" are injectable products, usually sold as melanotan, that people use to darken their skin without long sun exposure. They are synthetic analogues of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), the hormone that signals skin cells to make melanin, and users take them to get a deeper, more even tan for a golden, healthier-looking complexion.[1][2]

On looksmax.org, users describe melanotan as a way to get tan quickly for an event or to keep a tan through darker months, often paired with some UV exposure from the sun or a tanning bed.[3] Others discuss its effect on freckles and on the colour of moles, and some compare it with self-tanning lotions.[4][5]

The products are not approved as tanning drugs. Health agencies began warning against them in 2007, and the US FDA issued a warning letter in 2009.[2] A 2009 BMJ report linked an unlicensed "sun tan jab" to changes in moles.[6] Related approved drugs exist for other uses: afamelanotide for a rare light-sensitivity disorder and bremelanotide for hypoactive sexual desire disorder in premenopausal women.[1]

paras: Alpha-MSH's role in pigmentation has been known since the 1960s, and University of Arizona researchers developed analogues in the 1980s, including afamelanotide, first called melanotan I.[1] Melanotan I was licensed to an Australian start-up, Epitan, which became Clinuvel in 2006.[1] Melanotan II was later licensed to Palatin for sexual dysfunction, with development shifting around 2000 to bremelanotide.[2]
Gym and salon sales of products labelled melanotan began to draw regulator attention in 2007.[1][2]

Forum posts describe melanotan as a route to a darker tone for people who burn easily or want a tan in winter, with users saying that sun or tanning-bed exposure deepens the result.[3] One guide-style thread estimates that the peptide alone gives a small colour change and that most of the visible effect needs UV, a claim stated by the poster rather than established in trials.[3]

Threads also ask whether it darkens freckles, with replies saying it does and that freckles can be considered attractive.[4] Another thread asks whether the benefits are outweighed by the risks, with replies describing it as useful for a short period before an event.[7] Users also discuss nasal versus injected forms and other products such as self-tanner as alternatives.[3][7]

Reported effects include facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, yawning and appetite loss, and spontaneous erections in men.[2] Moles and freckles may darken.[2] The 2009 BMJ report described changes to moles linked to an unlicensed tan jab.[6]

Evidence on melanoma is unclear: a 2013 review found no conclusive proof of a causal link, and a 2021 review suggested higher melanoma rates among users could probably be explained by greater UV exposure.[2] Warnings were issued by agencies including the Danish Medicines Agency, UK MHRA, US FDA, Irish Medicines Board and Norwegian Medicines Agency.[2] The products are described as unlicensed in all jurisdictions.[1]

Other sunless options include DHA-based self-tanners and sprays, which colour the outer skin layer and fade over about five to ten days, and temporary bronzers that wash off.[1] Oral carotenoid products can tint the skin but have been the subject of FDA warnings when sold for tanning.[1]

No studies found for unlicensed tanning use. The 2009 BMJ item is a case report of mole changes.[6] Afamelanotide has been studied in trials for light-sensitivity conditions, which is a separate medical use.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, melanotan is discussed as a tanning shortcut, with threads on freckles, hair and brow colour, and whether risks outweigh rewards.[3][4][7]

claims.claim: Melanotan gives a tan with little or no sun.
It darkens freckles, which some users find attractive.
It is worth using briefly for an event.
